passages.note: Campaign page says in the third person that 'A Hilton administration will end state support for High-Speed Rail on Day 1'; a transit cut with no stated split against road capacity is direction at most, and the voice is not first person.
Debate remarks on the gas tax ('the worst roads in the country') and a promised veto of a mileage tax concern transportation revenue, not where investment goes between roads and other modes.
DMV plan strips 'transportation add-ons' from registration and seeks 'better value for money for spending on roads', which is cost efficiency, not the split between road capacity and other modes.
Plan to set VMT mitigation credits at zero is a fee rule on housing development (land use), not transportation investment.
New-cities plan mentions roads and 'modern transportation' designed into new communities but sets no priority between road capacity and walking, cycling or transit.
Housing-fee cap plan mentions how roads are paid for in new development; it is a land-use and fee rule, not a transportation investment split.
CHP funding and staffing plan concerns policing, not transportation investment.
Debate remarks on housing, climate, gas prices and EVs say nothing about investment in roads versus other modes.
The high-speed-rail pledge page captured only the site title; no text to code.

rows.reasoning: The only on-question passage is the campaign page's third-person promise that 'A Hilton administration will end state support for High-Speed Rail on Day 1'; it is not his own words, and a transit cut alone would show direction at most, not whether road capacity and traffic flow come first or roads are merely maintained. His own debate words on the gas tax and a mileage-tax veto concern revenue, not where investment goes between road capacity and pedestrian, cycling and transit options.
